Maju Forest, Gillman Barracks: Fewer homes and more greenery retained in revised housing plans
article:
HDB has revised the conceptual plans for the proposed housing developments at the Maju Forest and Gillman Barrack sites to allocate more land for greenery and reduce the development footprints by about 1,200 homes.

This follows environmental studies for both sites, a heritage study for Gillman Barracks, and feedback from the public and stakeholders.

In total, both sites are expected to yield around 11,000 homes over the next decade, HDB said on Oct 28.

This comprises roughly 4,000 public housing units at Maju Forest at Sunset Way, and some 7,000 homes at Gillman Barracks. The latter includes about 5,500 HDB flats.

That works out to a reduction of 400 flats at Maju Forest and 800 units at Gillman Barracks as compared to the original plans.

These are estimates based on broad planning assumptions and will need to be further studied at the detailed design stage, HDB noted.

Now that more land will be set aside for greenery, HDB said it also intends to efficiently use the remaining development area to provide new homes, such as by building taller blocks.

More details, such as the housing mix and launch dates, will be shared when ready.

Meanwhile, about 10ha, or 45%, of the Maju Forest site will be retained as greenery. That is up from around 8ha, or 35%, initially.

"The additional retained green area at the southern part of the site will result in a wider and more contiguous green area that will strengthen ecological connectivity within the site and along the Clementi Nature Corridor," said HDB.

And at Gillman Barracks, the area set aside for greenery will increase from 8ha, or 40% of the existing greenery in the area, to about 12ha, or 60%.

More of the existing forest around the hillock will be retained, which will provide a greener frontage towards Telok Blangah Street 31. The north-south ecological corridor along Lock Road and Malan Road will also be widened.

"These refinements will enhance the ecological connectivity within the Southern Ridges, as well as towards Berlayar Creek and Labrador Nature Reserve," HDB said.

The National Parks Board (NParks) will also safeguard a "significant portion" of the greenery at both sites as nature parks, to enhance nature conservation, the housing authority added.

In reviewing the housing plans for both sites, government agencies weighed the ecological importance of retaining more greenery against housing needs and other land use considerations, given the circumstances of each site.

The public consultation period ran from July 10 to Aug 6, during which HDB received about 7,200 feedback submissions for Maju Forest and 2,300 for Gillman Barracks.

In addition, about a thousand stakeholders — including nature groups, youths, academics, planning and built-environment professionals — were engaged. Local grassroots advisers also spoke with residents living near both sites.

The initial announcement of the proposed housing developments on July 10 had caused a stir, with months of vigorous debate about issues including environmental conservation, ecology, climate resilience, heritage, housing demand, alternative sites, as well as the planning process and public participation.

Petitions calling for the protections of the sites reportedly attracted more than 50,000 signatures in total.

title: Top 6 Temasek-Linked Blue-Chip Stocks to Watch This Week
article:
Results season for
Singapore real estate investment trusts
(S-REITs) lands at the end of October.
Following up on our earlier piece examining the
top three Temasek-linked blue chips
to watch this week, we are turning our attention to the next three key names on the radar.
These three S-REITs report within two days of each other.
Company
Ticker
Reporting date
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (CICT)
SGX: C38U
Thursday, 29 October 2026
CapitaLand Ascendas REIT (CLAR)
SGX: A17U
Thursday, 29 October 2026
Mapletree Pan Asia Commercial Trust (MPACT)
SGX: N2IU
Friday, 30 October 2026
Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore, held a deemed interest of 21.4% in CICT as at 27 February 2026.
It held a deemed interest of 18.6% in CLAR as at 3 March 2026, and 56.91% in MPACT as at 30 June 2026.
A big shareholder doesn’t decide what lands in your account, though.
The per-unit numbers do.
Each REIT heads into this week with a different question.
Can CICT keep its DPU growth ahead of growth in its unit base?
CICT is Singapore’s largest REIT by market capitalisation.
It owns retail, office and integrated development properties, with total assets of S$28.2 billion as at 30 June 2026.
For the first half of 2026 (1H2026), gross revenue rose 7.5% year on year (YoY) to S$846.8 million, while net property income (NPI) climbed 8.7% to S$630.5 million.
Distribution per unit (DPU) grew 7.1% to S$0.0602.
Here’s the thing: CICT’s unit base grew 5.8%, and yet DPU still came out ahead.
Portfolio occupancy rose 0.4 percentage points quarter on quarter to 95.6%.
Retail occupancy hit 97.7%, above the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s (URA) islandwide figure of 93.5%.
Rental reversions stayed positive at 4.0% for retail and 6.5% for office.
So what’s new this time? Paragon.
CICT completed the S$3.9 billion acquisition on 1 July 2026, just after the half ended, so watch for its first contribution.
The sale of Asia Square Tower 2, for net proceeds of about S$2.45 billion, is expected to be completed in 2H2026.
Aggregate leverage improved to 37.4% as at 30 June 2026, and average cost of debt held steady at 2.9% – though both figures precede Paragon’s completion.
Related articles:
Keppel DC REIT vs CICT: Which REIT Would I Buy Today?
Unlocking CICT’s Growth Engine: From AEIs to a S$1.1B Hougang Expansion
When will CLAR’s income growth reach unitholders?
CLAR is a diversified industrial REIT with 234 properties across Singapore, Australia, the US, the UK/Europe and Japan, and a portfolio valued at S$20.1 billion as at 30 June 2026.
In 1H2026, gross revenue rose 6.7% YoY to S$805.5 million, and NPI grew 6.2% to S$556.1 million.
Total distributable income expanded 8.6% to S$359.4 million.
However, DPU rose by just 0.1% YoY to S$0.07482.
Why the gap?
Equity fundraisings in 1H2025 and 1H2026 lifted the number of units entitled to distributions by 8.5%, and the new units absorbed most of the income growth.
To put it simply, CLAR earned more, but each unit’s share barely moved.
Occupancy slipped to 89.1% from 91.8% a year ago.
For context, part of the decline reflects the addition of two newly completed properties.
Excluding them, occupancy would have been 90.3%.
Rental reversions came in at 8.5% for 1H2026, and management expects them to stay positive in the high single digits for the full year.
CLAR has also announced a further S$638.1 million in acquisitions and plans to divest Kim Chuan Telecommunications Complex for S$200.4 million, representing a 32% premium to its valuation.
Aggregate leverage stood at 39.7%, the highest of the three REITs, with cost of debt at 3.5%.
Related articles:
STI Downturn: 3 Temasek-Linked S-REITs to Watch
CICT vs CapitaLand Ascendas REIT: Which CapitaLand Giant Is the Better Buy?
Can VivoCity keep carrying MPACT?
MPACT owns 15 commercial properties across Singapore, Hong Kong, China, Japan and South Korea, with assets under management of S$15.2 billion as at 30 June 2026.
Its latest figures cover just one quarter, the first quarter of the fiscal year ending 31 March 2027 (1QFY2027).
Gross revenue fell 5.6% YoY to S$206.5 million, and NPI dropped 6.8% to S$154.8 million.
DPU declined a milder 2.5% to S$0.0196, as an 18.4% drop in finance expenses softened the blow.
VivoCity remains the bright spot.
Its NPI rose 8.9% YoY, helped by the completed Basement 2
asset enhancement
, positive rental reversions of 13.5% and step-up rents.
On the flip side, the weaker spots sit mostly outside Singapore.
Portfolio committed occupancy fell to 84.4% from 89.3%. Japan, at 56.0%, and China, at 82.4%, dragged the figure lower.
Rental reversions came in at −9.1% for Festival Walk and −29.2% for China.
The absence of income from divested assets and a stronger Singapore dollar also weighed on the quarter.
That leaves the payout leaning on VivoCity and lower finance costs.
A recovery in overseas NPI would put it on firmer ground.
Watch Festival Walk’s 18,800-square-foot reconfiguration, which became operational in July 2026.
MPACT puts its return on investment at close to 50%, though on a small outlay of about HK$5.3 million.
Aggregate leverage stood at 37.7%, and cost of debt improved to 2.94%.
Related articles:
5 High-Yield Singapore Stocks: Are Their Dividends Really Safe?
5 Best Singapore REITs Income Investors Can Watch for 2H
Get Smart: Look past the headline total
When the updates land, put the total next to the per-unit figure.
If distributable income grows faster than DPU, find out where the difference went.
CLAR’s 1H2026 results show how new units can soak up income growth.
MPACT’s 1QFY2027 results show how lower finance costs can prop up a payout even as property income falls.
Temasek’s stake tells you who owns these REITs, but the per-unit number tells you what they pay you.
So when the updates arrive, ask each one a question: did the growth reach you per unit?

title: Mercedes readies major China overhaul as slump deepens
article:
(Oct 28): Mercedes-Benz Group AG is preparing a broader overhaul of its China strategy after the luxury-car market deteriorated more sharply than expected, insisting it has no plans to retreat from what remains the world’s largest auto market.

Chief executive officer Ola Källenius said conditions in China are “deteriorating beyond what we had thought would happen this year”, with weakness intensifying further in the second half. The downturn has been particularly severe at the upper end of the market, where Mercedes has traditionally held a strong position and generated some of its richest margins.

Källenius said Mercedes is reviewing everything from its product line-up to sales, production, sourcing and technology in China, with a broader strategy to be presented in 2027.

“There is not a play where you put China aside,” he told analysts on Wednesday. “It has to be one of the pillars of your strategy.”

The reassessment comes as Mercedes pushes ahead with its biggest product and cost overhaul in years. Third-quarter revenue fell 4.5% to €30.7 billion (US$34.1 billion or $43.8 billion), while adjusted group earnings before interest and tax declined 15%, the German carmaker said on Wednesday. A day earlier, Mercedes lowered its outlook, citing a worsening China slump and higher costs.

At the core cars division, adjusted earnings more than halved to €560 million in the third quarter, and the margin narrowed to 2.5% from 4.8%, reflecting the weaker contribution from China as well as currency and product-launch costs.

See also: Pop Mart's 3Q sales fall up to 50% as Labubu fad cools

Mercedes vehicle sales in China fell 31% in the third quarter from a year earlier, extending a decline driven by weaker luxury demand, fierce price competition and increasingly sophisticated domestic rivals.

Mercedes shares fell less than 1% on Wednesday in Frankfurt, following Tuesday’s 3.9% decline. The stock has lost more than a third of its value this year.

See also: China’s 5-year government bond yield trades near record low

Källenius said Mercedes isn’t treating the decline as a reason to downgrade China to a niche market. Beyond its sheer size, the country remains important because of its fast-moving technology ecosystem and the growing global reach of Chinese suppliers and automakers, he said.

The company is instead trying to remake the economics of selling cars there. A coming electric E-Class was developed from what Källenius described as effectively a “white sheet of paper”, with a product tailored more closely to Chinese buyers and sourcing shifted much more heavily into the country.

Mercedes will get close to sourcing the vehicle entirely in China for local production, Källenius said, helping cut variable costs significantly compared with its previous model. The company also plans to price the car realistically for local market conditions rather than relying on the economics that underpinned its China business in the past.

Still, Källenius ruled out chasing volume at any cost. Mercedes won’t adopt the “fire sale market-share-at-all-cost” approach pursued by some competitors, he said, underscoring the tension between protecting the brand and competing in one of the world’s fiercest price wars.

Chief financial officer Harald Wilhelm said the company expects its new-model momentum to strengthen further in 2027, alongside continued reductions in variable costs. But he declined to predict where China will be by then, saying the company would give a clearer assessment when it reports full-year results in February.

The comments add to signs that Mercedes increasingly sees China as a structural challenge rather than a temporary cyclical downturn. For years, CEO Ola Källenius has pursued a strategy centered on selling fewer but more expensive cars, relying heavily on models such as the S-Class, Maybach, G-Class and AMG range to support margins.

That calculation has become harder as China’s property downturn weighs on luxury spending and local rivals challenge Mercedes on price, software, electric technology and increasingly design.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Mercedes is responding with both cost cuts and its largest-ever product offensive. More than 40 new or refreshed models are due by the end of 2027. The electric CLA and GLC are already being rolled out, with new versions of the C-Class, S-Class, GLE and GLS among the vehicles intended to revive demand.

The company is also targeting material-cost savings of around 8% compared with 2024 levels, with substantially deeper reductions planned in China, and is shrinking an industrial footprint built for stronger volumes. Voluntary redundancy programmes are being used to reduce the German workforce.

The pressure extends across Germany’s auto industry. BMW AG and Volkswagen AG have also warned that deteriorating conditions in China are hurting earnings, highlighting how quickly a market that once generated outsized profits has become one of the sector’s biggest structural problems.

Volvo Car AB CEO Håkan Samuelsson said last week that the market for Western-developed cars in China isn’t coming back.

title: Hong Lai Huat sets up investment subsidiary in Singapore, eyes real estate opportunities
article:
Mainboard-listed Hong Lai Huat Group has incorporated Huat Assets Management, a new wholly owned subsidiary in Singapore. The subsidiary will identify and pursue investment opportunities across various real estate sectors in Singapore, according to an Oct 28 bourse filing.

The incorporation forms part of the group’s ongoing efforts to explore suitable real estate investment opportunities in Singapore, according to Hong Lai Huat.

With the aim of generating recurring rental income and achieving long-term capital appreciation, Huat Assets Management’s investment activities “may include property acquisitions, asset management, strategic divestments, asset enhancement and redevelopment opportunities, where commercially viable”.

The group is currently evaluating suitable investment opportunities in Singapore.

The property developer currently holds two completed projects in Cambodia: D’Seaview, which has 737 residential units and 67 commercial units. Royal Platinum, which is a joint venture, has 851 residential units and 50 commercial units.

The company has previously been involved in various boutique condominium projects across Singapore’s eastern region. Speaking to The Edge Singapore in June, Hong Lai Huat executive director and chief strategy officer Dylan Ong said the group will be looking at potential land banks in Singapore for boutique residential development.

See also: Hong Lai Huat maintains property focus despite marble mining bonanza in Cambodia

Shares in Hong Lai Hut closed 3.5% higher at 6 cents on Oct 28, down some 25% year to date.

title: Adani flagship returns to profit as newer businesses deliver
article:
(Oct 28): Billionaire Gautam Adani-controlled Adani Enterprises Ltd returned to profit in the second quarter as newer businesses including airports and data centres scaled up.

Net income was 14.9 billion rupees for the three months ended Sept 30, according to an exchange filing on Wednesday. While that is 55% lower than the year-ago profit, the performance marks a return to black after the company had reported a loss of 11.6 billion rupees in the previous quarter amid costs linked to settlement of US legal cases.

Revenue climbed 75% year-on-year to 372.2 billion rupees and costs rose 71% to 360.2 billion rupees, the filing showed. Shares of the Adani Group flagship slipped 0.4% after the earnings were announced, in line with the fall in the S&P BSE Sensex.

The return to profitability could ease investor concerns about funding requirements for expansion and that newer businesses are approaching an earnings inflection point. Airports, data centres, roads and clean-energy ventures are expected to play a growing role in Adani Enterprises’ profit mix as they start generating cash flow.

Revenue from the integrated resources management — a unit that mostly consists of coal trading and contributes the most to the company’s overall revenue — rose 6.6% to 70.97 billion rupees. The airports business is surging in the mix, with its revenue rising 15% to nearly 37 billion rupees. New energy and commercial mining units also posted rising revenue from year-ago period.

See also: Chinese EV imports surge in Thailand ahead of planned excise tax

Gross debt for Adani Enterprises slipped 0.3% from the preceding quarter to 972.94 billion rupees.

In May, the US Department of Justice dropped criminal bribery charges against Gautam Adani and his nephew, Sagar Adani, after they agreed to pay US$18 million to settle a parallel civil fraud case there.

See also: Universal Music discussed going private with buyout firms

The ports-to-power conglomerate accelerated its growth plans after resolving its legal troubles in the US. In May, the Department of Justice dropped criminal bribery charges against Adani and his nephew, Sagar Adani, after they agreed to pay US$18 million to settle a parallel civil fraud case there. Separately, Adani Enterprises paid US$275 million to resolve a sanctions probe by the Office of Foreign Assets Control. Neither the executives nor the company admitted wrongdoing.

Drawing a line under its US regulatory probes stoked a 43% rally for the stock earlier this year but the shares have tumbled more than 20% from their peak in July, wiping out almost US$10 billion in market value.

The growth prospects for its airport and copper businesses, as well as its joint venture with Jabil for artificial intelligence and data centre equipment manufacturing will stay in focus for investors in the coming months, with consensus expectations for the stock to rally more than 40% in the next 12 months.

title: Asia leads US-friendly nations in cutting their purchases of Treasury by 60%
article:
(Oct 28): Being one of Washington’s closest partners no longer means reliably funding the US deficit.

Countries and regions most aligned with the US bought a net US$174.3 billion of Treasuries, excluding bills, in the first eight months of 2026, according to an analysis of Treasury and State Department data. That was the lowest for the period since 2021 and down more than 60% from a year earlier.

The shift is noteworthy in Asia, where economies running large surpluses are putting less of that money into US debt. Japan, the biggest foreign holder of Treasuries, bought just US$389 million in the first eight months — down 99% from a year earlier. South Korea sold US$23.8 billion, the most for the period in records going back to 1977. Taiwan was also a net seller.

There’s no single explanation for the shift. Governments have said little about any plans to move away from Treasuries, and the data don’t separate government buying from private investment at the country level. Several factors may be contributing, including weak currencies, rising yields at home, growing demand for stocks and unease over US policy.

“The Treasury market isn’t losing foreign buyers — it’s losing automatic buyers,” said Masahiko Loo, a senior fixed-income strategist at State Street Investment Management, which oversees over US$6 trillion. “An increasingly unpredictable US makes large structural overweights and the automatic recycling of capital into Treasuries harder to justify.”

See also: AI tech fears push global credit spreads to 17-month high

The US government’s debt pile has climbed past US$40 trillion, leaving the world’s largest economy more reliant on investors to fund its spending. At the same time, President Donald Trump’s tariffs and uncertainty over US policy have spurred concerns about the dollar’s longer-term outlook. And with yields rising in markets from Japan to Europe, global investors have more alternatives to Treasuries than they once did.

Asia’s big savers have typically converted their surpluses into dollars and parked the money in Treasuries. This year, weakening currencies eroded their buying power and pushed governments to dip into reserves.

The yen sank to its weakest level in four decades, and data suggested Tokyo sold some of its Treasuries and other securities over the summer as it sought to support the currency. The won fell to its lowest since 2009 before recovering.

See also: Paris unrest poses contamination risks to bond yields beyond France

Governments haven’t shed much light on their approach. In May, a senior Japanese Finance Ministry official suggested that selling Treasuries to prop up the yen is counterproductive, saying authorities are mindful of the risks of selling their holdings. The Bank of Korea said in September it plans to broaden investments beyond US bonds for a portion of its reserves managed by domestic asset managers.

Alignment can be subjective. This analysis, an update of one first published in February, classifies countries as most-, least- and neutrally-aligned by how often their votes on key United Nations resolutions match those of the US, using State Department data. The approach is commonly used in academia to determine allies and adversaries.

For example, longtime military ally Australia was classified as most-aligned, China as least, with America’s neighbour Mexico falling into the neutral bucket.

The figures are net purchases — buying minus selling — of Treasuries with an original maturity of more than one year. They cover 57 countries and regions and include both official and private investors.

The Treasury data may attribute securities to the country where they are held through custodians or intermediaries, rather than to the nation of the ultimate owner. Holdings and purchases attributed to financial centers such as the UK and Belgium may therefore partly reflect investors elsewhere.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Even when Asian money is flowing overseas, Treasuries aren’t necessarily the default first choice.

Korean investors prefer stocks, while Taiwan’s money has shifted towards equities and deposits, according to Brad Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former US Treasury official. “So some friends with big surpluses haven’t been big net buyers,” he said.

Setser sees this as part of a broader “dereservification” trend, in which more foreign assets are held outside traditional central-bank reserves and instead flow through pension funds, state banks and other large institutions. That doesn’t amount to de-dollarisation, but can mean less “official demand” for Treasuries, according to Setser.

"Elevated dollar funding rates continue to erode returns on Treasuries just as rising domestic yields have improved opportunities in JGBs," says Andre de Silva, Markets Live strategist at Bloomberg Strategists.

Higher yields elsewhere are also giving investors options. Korea’s Kiwoom Asset Management remains cautious on Treasuries and sees Japanese government bonds as relatively attractive, said Yang Joo Kyung, head of global fixed income.

Japanese investors have more reason to keep their money at home too. With domestic yields at multi-decade highs, the extra return they can earn from investing overseas has narrowed.

“Japan is a US ally, and we’ve certainly seen some signs that there is a kind of gradual unwind of the carry trade,” said Oliver Levingston, G10 foreign-exchange and rates strategist at BofA Securities, referring to the practice of borrowing cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere.

That doesn’t mean the US is running out of buyers. Private investors, including hedge funds, banks and mutual funds, have stepped in, boosting their share of federal debt to about 70%, near the highest since 1990.

But they’re more sensitive to price. For Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh, that means markets can react sharply if investors grow uneasy about monetary policy, the economy, widening US deficits or signals coming from the White House.

That sensitivity contributed to benchmark 10-year yields rising above 5% this year. They climbed about three basis points to 5.02% on Wednesday.

The countries least aligned with Washington bought US$17.1 billion of Treasuries from January through August, reversing four straight years of selling over the same period. That’s a tenth of what US-aligned countries bought.

China remains the biggest seller, ahead of Korea, though some analysts believe Beijing might have channeled some transactions through other nations, including Canada. Belgium — whose holdings are thought to include some Chinese accounts — ranked third. The UK, Hong Kong and India were the biggest buyers.

“China’s continued reductions are consistent with a longer-term diversification trend, even as the underlying motivations are harder to establish,” said Laura Cooper, London-based head of macro credit at Nuveen.

This isn’t the first time US-aligned countries have pulled back from Treasuries. They sold sharply in 2020, when the Covid-19 pandemic triggered a global scramble for liquidity.

Even so, the US$32 trillion Treasury market remains unmatched in its depth, liquidity and near round-the-clock trading, while the dollar retains its role as the world’s dominant reserve currency.

Foreigners still owned US$7.85 trillion of Treasuries as of August, near an all-time high, though their share of the market has shrunk to less than a third from a peak of 52% in 2012.

“When you look at the alternatives, they’re pretty few and far between,” said Robert Tipp, head of global bonds at PGIM. “So you have had a rebalancing and consistent runoff from some countries, but it’s been absorbed by others.”

Foreign investors aren’t abandoning US assets either. Some of that money is shifting into American equities and corporate debt, suggesting investors remain keen on US companies even as appetite for government debt cools.

And the buyers filling the gap are likely to demand more compensation than the friendly nations that used to fund Washington with little fuss.

“The Treasury will fund itself — the question is the price and the volatility of the price,” said Shoki Omori, Deutsche Bank AG’s chief fixed-income strategist for Japan. “What the level cannot buy back is the patient, price-insensitive money the allies used to supply.”

title: Danone sales rise on higher prices, medical nutrition demand
article:
(Oct 28): Danone SA sales climbed in the third quarter, driven by higher prices and persistent demand for its protein-rich yoghurts and fortified drinks for the elderly and ill.

Like-for-like sales rose 4%, the producer of Oikos Greek yoghurt said in a statement Wednesday, above the 3.7% estimate of analysts in a Bloomberg survey. Increased pricing added 3.6% to sales growth — a bigger share than expected — while volume growth lagged.

The specialised nutrition unit showed the strongest jump in sales, topping estimates on strength in Asia and the Americas. A poor performance linked to adverse weather hit the Mizone waters business in Asia, shaving a percentage point off group sales growth in the quarter.

The results are “a mixed bag", Jefferies analysts led by David Hayes said in a note.

The shares rose as much as 2.7% in early Paris trading. The stock was down 20% this year through Tuesday’s close, trailing rival Nestle SA and on course for the worst annual performance since 2020.

CEO Antoine de Saint-Affrique has led a turnaround in five years atop the company by shedding weaker businesses and expanding in areas like high-protein dairy offerings and food for cancer patients. The rise of weight-loss drugs has spurred demand for protein-rich, gut-friendly products.

See also: What to know about plague after suspected Russia lab worker case

Still, weakness in the US has weighed on sentiment. Danone announced a host of changes to boost performance in the US “with a sense of urgency", deputy CEO Juergen Esser told investors Wednesday. “We are obviously not satisfied with this performance in light of a market which is growing faster.”

Danone has added production capacity of high-protein yoghurts at four of its US factories and will continue to add more. “Capacity is at the end of Q3 no longer a limiting factor to our growth,” Esser said.

Another change is new leadership, bringing Francois Lacombe from Danone’s Spanish business across to the US. Danone next year will also launch kefir, fibre-enriched products and a new natural Greek yoghurt to add to its existing “performance” Greek yoghurt brand, Oikos.

See also: PRECISE and AWS to build systems for Singapore’s 450,000-person genomics study

Danone confirmed its guidance to increase like-for-like sales between 3% and 5% this year, with recurring operating income growing faster than sales.

Earlier this year, Danone agreed to buy UK-based Huel, a maker of fortified protein powders and ready-to-consume drinks and meals popular with gym-goers. It also acquired Australian dairy company Made Group to expand its offerings of coconut water and protein shakes in Asia.
